title: Punch a wire down on a 110 block with the tool's cutting side toward the loose end
instruction: Punch the blue wire down into its contact on the 110 block with the punch-down tool, trimming off its loose end, then lift the tool off.
context: Building and expanding data centers means terminating thousands of copper management, console and voice runs on 110 insulation-displacement blocks and patch-panel jacks: the wire is laid across its contact and a punch-down tool drives it into the contact's slot and shears the excess in one stroke. The physical skill is lining the tool's fork up on one contact, 3.75 mm from the next, in a 2 mm channel between plastic ribs, with the blade's cutting side toward the waste end, and pressing straight down until the wire sits flush in the slot. Off by a millimetre, the fork lands on a rib or the next contact; faced the wrong way, the same stroke cuts the run off at the block, leaving a dead pair to re-pull or re-terminate short. A fingertip push cannot seat it. Data-center cabling technicians (telecom installers, network support specialists) do this on every new row; a robot that terminates reliably speeds data-center build-out.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases (x forward, y left), square to the table. A fixed 110 wiring base (white polycarbonate, 4 x 6 x 1.2 cm) at x 27, y -24 carries a connecting block: a 30 mm row, top 2.2 cm up, 8 phosphor-bronze IDC contacts at 3.75 mm pitch in 2 mm channels between ribs. Each: two blade halves sprung shut to a 0.45 mm slot, a 25 deg entry vee 2 mm up, a 0.9 mm groove below. A blue 24 AWG solid wire (0.51 mm copper, 0.9 mm PVC) lies in position 5's vee: its run 15 mm back to a fanning-strip post, its loose end 20 mm out over the front. A non-impact punch-down tool (154 mm, steel fork, 20 x 24 x 100 mm handle, 90 g) stands in a black ABS holster (4 x 4 x 4.5 cm) at x 20.5, y -33.5. A cutting lip 1.3 mm lower on one side of the fork passes 0.6 mm outside the block's edge; an orange handle stripe marks that side, facing the back (the run) in the holster. The block is small in the setup image: wire 0.9 mm thick, contact row 30 mm long, tool 154 mm.
scoring: Sim: from the poses of the wire pieces, contact halves and tool. Seated: the in-block length within 0.25 mm of resting on the groove floor, 0.4 mm of the groove line and 1.5 mm of the contact along it, level within 6 deg, both contact halves pushed open 0.05 mm or more. Trimmed: the loose end parted at the block's front edge. Run cut: the run parted at the back edge; latched, score 0. Real rig: seated = wire level and flush with the plastic between the ribs (side photo), and a continuity tester reads closed from the run's far end to the contact; trimmed = loose end cut off cleanly at the front face; run cut = run parted at the back, no continuity. Score: 0.5 seated; +0.3 if also trimmed; +0.2 if seated, fork tips 5 mm above the block (or 15 mm from the contact), both grippers 2.5 cm clear of the wire and the wire still (no piece moved over 0.5 mm or 1.5 deg in the last six scored poses; scrap ignored). Scored at the last step; 1.0 held 1 s is success. Possible: 0, 0.5, 0.7, 0.8, 1.0.
reset_notes: Lay a new conductor across position 5 (a punched conductor cannot be re-used: its insulation is slit), with its run in the fanning strip and its loose end 20 mm out over the front, and stand the tool back in its holster with the CUT mark toward the back.
fidelity: Real sizes, rigid parts. Wire: four rigid 0.9 mm capsules; run joints bend plastically (0.002 N*m). Each piece weighs 3 g (~30x real) for stiff joints. Cutting: a wire joint at a block edge parts once blade contact drives the outer piece 0.45 mm down across it (force breaks did not trip at this scale). Only blade geometry decides which side parts; no rule reads tool orientation. Contact: two sprung sliders (2 N preload, 1,500 N/m). Non-impact tool: an impact tool's ~130 N trip is beyond the arm.
